title: Year covariance raised estimated mean-slope errors for England and Wales Meadow Brown dates in 1985-2024
abstract: We tested the precision of the mean spring temperature slope for Meadow Brown flight dates in England and Wales. We used separate country models in 1985-2004 and 2005-2024, with site effects and linear time. Keeping shared-year covariance raised the estimated standard error of the equal-weight mean slope by 27% and 33%. The increase persisted with high-count records, common sites, count adjustment and short serial dependence. Adding summer temperature reduced but did not remove the increase. In the later period, the marginal 95% mean-slope interval crossed zero only when covariance was kept. These are model-based precision comparisons, not known true errors. Only 20 years per period, few Welsh sites, missing visit histories and weather-dependent detection limit inference. Shared residual conditions can explain covariance; common temperature alone need not do so. No causal climate or pollution effect is identified. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes and a retrieval recipe are supplied.

display.caption: Country spring slopes with marginal 95% intervals, and standard errors for their equal-weight mean. Keeping shared-year covariance raises estimated errors in both periods. Contains UKBMS data; source attribution is in README.md.

citations.reason: Prior Meadow Brown timing models noted shared weather. We audit cross-country covariance with overlapping biological source data and new country weather models.
